los: Distinguish a platform feature from an affordance or constraint relative to a named learner action.
Build an action-to-affordance map that classifies each platform response as affordance, soft constraint, or hard constraint, and re-run the classification across learner variability.
Choose among redesigning the action, changing the tool, or keeping the constraint on purpose when an action hits a hard constraint, with a stated learning reason.
Verify an affordance against the live tool rather than assuming it from a feature name or marketing copy.
ail606/02/02.description: AIL 606 textbook section on platform affordances and constraints: building an action-to-affordance map, distinguishing soft from hard constraints, reading signifiers, and verifying affordances against the live tool, with reader notes, support moments, and revision evidence.

los: Match a cognitive operation (compare, sequence, decide, observe) to the interaction pattern whose structure enacts it (interaction-cognition fit).
Diagnose an interaction for split attention, seductive detail, or interaction-cost asymmetry.
Verify that an interaction closes its loop with a visible consequence and stays equitable for keyboard and screen-reader learners.
Defend a pattern choice with behavioral evidence and a named rejected alternative rather than production value.
Diagnose whether a practice loop feeds forward using Hattie and Timperley's three questions, and rewrite a bare verdict into actionable feedback.
Choose a feedback-reveal timing (immediate versus brief delay) justified by task type and learner expertise.
Design calibrated learner control that preserves autonomy while naming the cost of skipping.
Tie each loop revision to a behavioral signal such as repeat-error rate, skip rate, or retry uptake.
Classify an optimizer suggestion as goal-aligned, goal-neutral, or goal-opposed by reading its mechanism before its predicted-gain magnitude.
Explain why engagement proxies (completion, time-on-page, efficiency) cannot on their own certify that learning occurred, using Goodhart's law.
Defend an accessibility provision against an efficiency edit on UDL learner-variability grounds the usage metric cannot see.
Produce a triaged optimizer report with a per-row verdict and mechanism, at least one reasoned rejection, and a before-after transfer check on the accepted edit.
Build a comparative audit matrix that scores every candidate tool on the same task-derived criteria.
Distinguish a pass-or-fail gate from a weighted dimension and apply gates before reading totals.
State a recommendation bounded by its named context (learners, budget, constraints) plus the re-entry condition that would change the winner.
Document a bounded AI/software support move with an accepted and a rejected suggestion, such as using BigAL to attack the criteria rather than rank the tools.

Convert a descriptive storyboard caption into a four-slot frame claim: prior state, predicted action with a learner verb, warrant tying a feature to a Mayer or cognitive-load principle, and disconfirming evidence.
Apply the three falsifiability tests (action, warrant, disconfirmation) to diagnose a frame claim.
Verify claim-chaining so that frame N's predicted action becomes frame N+1's prior state.
Judge an AI suggestion against the warrant standard, accepting or rejecting it with a stated reason.
Apply the scarcity and contrast law of signaling: justify cuing exactly one element on a frame and name the cues withheld.
Run the seam test to place a learner-controlled segmentation break at a conceptual boundary, distinguishing segmenting from pagination and from auto-advance.
Treat a signaling cue as a cognitive-load expenditure and judge an AI-proposed cue against its processing cost for a named learner.
Tie cue count and segment count to learner expertise (novice versus near-expert, expertise reversal) and document calibration as restraint in the storyboard trace.
State the representational function of an instructional image in one sentence before prompting.
Apply the function, coherence, and accuracy three-gate screen to a generated image and reject at the first failed gate.
Verify generated image content (labels, counts, proportions, and social representation) against an authoritative source, documenting an accepted and a rejected AI suggestion.
Distinguish prompt-craft polish from a function-first, verified image decision.
Diagnose why a storyboard peer comment fails by identifying which of the three properties (anchored, actionable, authorship-preserving) is missing.
Rewrite a praise or taste comment into a three-part review (observation, anchor, option) that cites a Mayer principle or the frame objective.
Explain why the author's documented accept-or-reject response, not the comment itself, is the design evidence, and why a principled rejection can be stronger than an acceptance.
Maintain anchored, authorship-preserving review across a power gradient, as in the senior-to-junior transfer case.

ail606/06/04.lo1_only: Conduct an analytic, criterion-referenced prototype quality review that scores severity independently of quality and orders revisions by severity, not by lowest score.

los: Convert praise or preference into criterion-anchored, actionable peer critique using the element-problem-criterion frame.
Respond to each critique point with a reasoned disposition (accept, modify, or reject), including at least one reasoned rejection.
Verify an AI-drafted critique against the actual artifact before adopting any of its points.
Use annotations, support requests, and revision notes to decide what help or design change should come next.
Treat a six-component capstone package as one argument and list every cross-component claim it makes.
Reconcile contradictory claims by correcting the inaccurate component toward the recorded evidence, not by inflating the log.
Verify any AI-assembled package summary against each underlying artifact before submitting.
Write a reflective synthesis naming how your design judgment changed across the module.
Diagnose why a rubric descriptor produces inter-rater disagreement by distinguishing adjective descriptors from observable, countable anchors.
Reconcile a rater split by tracing it to a feature of the work rather than averaging the scores.
Rewrite a level descriptor into a countable observation and verify the gain by re-scoring drafts and re-checking exact agreement.
Apply the new-rater test to judge whether reported agreement is calibration or convergence by habit.
Contrast deterrence and transparency models of academic integrity and explain why generative AI makes deterrence unenforceable.
Write an AI-use clause with a bounded permission, a one-line disclosure format with a worked example, and an accessibility carve-out.
Apply the distinguishability, disclosure-cost, and accessibility checks to evaluate a draft AI-use policy.
Predict the behavioral effect (concealment, exclusion, or transparency) a policy clause will produce.
Map each element of a prototype screen to a named WCAG 2.2 success criterion (1.1.1, 1.4.1, 1.4.3, 2.1.1, 2.2.1) rather than judging by appearance.
Prioritize accessibility fixes by depth of exclusion, fixing full lock-outs before strain.
Add redundant cues (color plus label plus icon) consistent with UDL learner variability without raising load for other learners.
Judge an AI-drafted alt text against WCAG 1.1.1 (does it name what the image shows and why it matters) before accepting it.
ail606/08/05.description: AIL 606 textbook section on running a WCAG-anchored accessibility review of a prototype: mapping elements to WCAG 2.2 success criteria, prioritizing fixes by depth of exclusion, and adding redundant cues for learner variability, with reader notes, support moments, and revision evidence.
